Title: Coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic
Commentary:
The percentage of people testing positive for COVID-19 continued to decrease in all four UK nations in the latest week (ending 27 February 2021). The hospital admissions rate in England also continued to decrease in the week ending 28 February. The number of registered deaths involving COVID-19 in England and Wales decreased in the week ending 26 February.

Around 1 in 4 people in England, 1 in 6 in Wales, 1 in 8 in Scotland and 1 in 6 in Northern Ireland had antibodies against COVID-19 in the 28 days to 11 February. The majority of adults in Great Britain (94%) said they had either received, are awaiting, or would be likely to have the COVID-19 vaccine if offered (24 to 28 February).

Title: Coronavirus (COVID-19) infections
Commentary: The percentage of people testing positive for COVID-19 has continued to decrease in all four UK nations (week ending 27 February 2021). In England around 1 in 220 people in the community population had COVID-19. Around 1 in 285 people were infected in Wales, 1 in 325 in Northern Ireland and 1 in 335 in Scotland. The North East had the highest infection rate of English regions.

Title: Hospital admissions with coronavirus (COVID-19)
Commentary:
Hospital admissions of COVID-19-confirmed patients in England decreased to 8.4 per 100,000 people in the week ending 28 February 2021. This is four times lower than rates seen in mid-January. In the most recent week, hospital admission rates decreased in all English regions and across all age groups.

Data on hospital admissions presented here are collected by Public Health England and available on the GOV.UK coronavirus dashboard and national flu and COVID-19 surveillance reports.

Data on coronavirus confirmed hospital admissions for other nations are available on Northern Ireland Department of Health webpage, Scottish Government webpage and Public Health Wales dashboard.

Title: Deaths involving coronavirus (COVID-19)
Commentary:
The number of all deaths registered in England and Wales in the week ending 26 February 2021 was 12,614. Nearly a quarter (2,914) of these deaths mentioned COVID-19 on the death certificate, a decrease from the previous week. However, the total number of deaths registered was 9.2% higher than the five-year average. In January, COVID-19 was the leading cause of death in both England and Wales.

Weekly death registrations for Scotland and Northern Ireland are produced and published by National Records of Scotland and Northern Ireland Statistics and Research Agency..

Title: Impact of coronavirus (COVID-19) on society
Commentary:
Compliance with preventative measures to slow the spread of COVID-19, such as hand washing and the use of face coverings, remained high in the latest week (24 to 28 February 2021, Great Britain). The proportion of adults who felt that life will return to normal in six months or less increased to 32% from 22% in the week before. All four personal well-being scores improved slightly compared with the previous week.

While both men and women spent more time working from home, women spent more time on unpaid childcare and household work throughout the pandemic.

Title: Impact of coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic on different age groups
Commentary: Coronavirus infection rates decreased in all age groups in the week ending 27 February 2021, except for secondary school-aged children (School Years 7 to 11) where the trend is uncertain. The percentage of people testing positive was the highest among adults aged 25 to 34 years and the lowest among those aged 70 years and over. Hospital admission rates decreased in all age groups in the week ending 28 February. The majority of deaths involving COVID-19 (66.3%) were in people aged 75 years and over in the week ending 26 February.

Title: Overview of coronavirus  (COVID-19) pandemic by UK geographic area
Commentary: The percentage of people testing positive for COVID-19 decreased in most English regions in the week ending 27 February 2021. COVID-19-confirmed hospital admission rates fell in all regions of England in the week ending 28 February. The number of deaths involving COVID-19 decreased in all English regions in the week ending 26 February for the fourth consecutive week. London has the highest antibody prevalence and the South West has the lowest.

Title: Impact of coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic on different ethnic groups
Commentary: People from ethnic minorities are more likely to test positive for COVID-19 compared with White ethnic groups. COVID-19 death rates are also higher for most ethnic minorities compared with White ethnic groups. This is in part because of the types of jobs and housing more common among ethnic minorities, but this does not completely explain the disparity. Black or Black British adults were more likely to report hesitancy to a COVID-19 vaccine compared with White adults. Further ethnicity statistics are available on the Ethnicity Facts and Figures website.

Title: Antibodies against coronavirus (COVID-19)
Commentary: Antibodies against COVID-19 suggest that a person previously had the infection or has been vaccinated. The percentage of people testing positive for antibodies increased to around 1 in 4 people in England, 1 in 6 people in Wales, 1 in 8 people in Scotland and 1 in 6 people in Northern Ireland in the 28 days to 11 February. People aged 80 years and over were most likely to test positive for antibodies in England. London had the highest antibody positivity among English regions.

Title: Coronavirus (COVID-19) vaccination
Commentary:
Positive vaccine sentiment has increased to 94% in the latest period (24 to 28 February), from 78% when the data were first collected (10 to 13 December 2020). Over the period 13 January to 7 February 2021, the proportion of adults reporting hesitancy towards a COVID-19 vaccination varied by characteristic, such as by age, ethnicity, health conditions and deprivation.

Official data on the number of people who have received a COVID-19 vaccination is collated by Public Health England and is available on the GOV.UK coronavirus dashboard.

Title: Coronavirus (COVID-19) and other health conditions
Commentary:
Dementia and Alzheimer's disease was the most common pre-existing condition among deaths due to COVID-19 in England and Wales in 2020. For deaths occurring in people aged under 65 years, obesity, diabetes and hypertensive diseases were mentioned over three times more often in COVID-19 deaths than in all-cause deaths.

Adults who were not clinically extremely vulnerable or did not have an underlying health condition were more likely to report hesitancy towards a COVID-19 vaccine than those who were clinically extremely vulnerable or had an underlying health condition, respectively.

Title: Coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic in educational settings
Commentary:
In December 2020, the COVID-19 Schools Infection Survey conducted their second round of testing in primary and secondary schools. This research was conducted in partnership with the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, and Public Health England.

Research conducted alongside higher education bodies in 2020 found most university students said their mental health had worsened as a result of the pandemic. Initial research using case studies from the Universities of Exeter and Loughborough found a peak in cases following the start of the 2020 Autumn Term. Although these statistics are experimental, and findings are not applicable nationwide, they provide important information that will inform further research.
